0a83466d4352.say: Turn it up to one point five, and they flatten. Memory drops to about forty percent, and even coffee gets a small chance. That's why the same question can get different answers. Temperature is a setting, not a property of the model.
0a83466d4352.heard: Turn it up to 1.5 and they flatten. Memory drops to about 40%, and even coffee gets a small chance. That's why the same question can get different answers. Temperature is a setting, not a property of the model.

c6858f7e7149.say: Back to zero point seven, and roll the dice. Each roll can pick a different word, but most of the time, it picks memory.
c6858f7e7149.heard: Back to 0.7 and roll the dice. Each roll can pick a different word, but most of the time it picks memory.

be4117cec03c.say: Why softmax? The model gives scores, but to pick a word, we need odds that add up to one hundred percent. Softmax keeps the order, never gives a word exactly zero, and changes smoothly, which training needs to work out which way to nudge each weight.
be4117cec03c.heard: Why Sopmax? The model gives scores, but to pick a word, we need odds that add up to 100%. Sopmax keeps the order, never gives a word exactly zero, and changes smoothly, which training needs to work out which way to nudge each weight.

8bfddf835822.say: Let's calculate it with three words. The scores, also called logits, are the raw numbers from the last layer: two for memory, one for disk, zero for time. Higher means a better fit. They can be any number, even negative.
8bfddf835822.heard: Let's calculate it with three words. The scores, also called loggets, are the raw numbers from the last layer: two for memory, one for disk, zero for time. Higher means a better fit. They can be any number, even negative.

d2c9391ef033.say: First, e to the power of each score. e is a fixed number, about two point seven one eight. e to the two is seven point three nine, e to the one is two point seven two, and e to the zero is one. The result is always positive, and each extra point of score multiplies it by two point seven.
d2c9391ef033.heard: First, e to the power of each score. E is a fixed number, about 2.718. e to the 2 is 7.39. E to the 1 is 2.72, and e to the 0 is 1. The result is always positive, and each extra point of score multiplies it by 2.7.

9cdbae482064.say: At temperature one, we divide each by the total. Seven point three nine, over eleven point one one, gives memory sixty-six and a half percent.
9cdbae482064.heard: At temperature 1, we divide each by the total. 7.39 over 11.11 gives memory 66.5%.

e38187e1b263.say: At temperature zero point five, we divide the scores by zero point five, which doubles them, to four, two, and zero. The gaps double, and memory gets eighty-six point seven percent.
e38187e1b263.heard: At temperature 0.5, we divide the scores by 0.5, which doubles them to 4, 2, and 0. The gaps double, and memory gets 86.7%.

5c633b78fc7a.say: Step nine: why long context is expensive. Every token leaves a key and a value behind, in every attention layer. They never change, so the engine stores them, instead of recomputing them. That store is the K V cache.
5c633b78fc7a.heard: Step 9. Why long context is expensive? Every token leaves a key and a value behind in every attention layer. They never change, so the engine stores them instead of recomputing them. That store is the KV cache.

f541aa530790.say: The cache grows with every token, and each new token also has to compare against all of it. So long conversations cost both memory and time.
f541aa530790.heard: The cash grows with every token, and each new token also has to compare against all of it. So long conversations cost both memory and time.

6a828dffd552.say: Here's what that means for this model, at two hundred thousand tokens. If all forty-eight layers used full attention, the cache would take eighteen point three gigabytes. This model needs four point six, because only twelve of its layers keep a K V cache.
6a828dffd552.heard: Here's what that means for this model at 200,000 tokens. If all 48 layers used full attention, the cache would take 18.3 gigabytes. This model needs 4.6 because only 12 of its layers keep a KV cache.

7794a174e85b.say: The arithmetic: twelve layers, times two heads, times two hundred and fifty-six numbers, times two for key and value, times two bytes. That's twenty-four kilobytes for every token. Keeping this number down is what most of part two is about.
7794a174e85b.heard: The arithmetic 12 layers times 2 heads times 256 numbers times 2 for key and value times 2 bytes. That's 24 kilobytes for every token. Keeping this number down is what most of part 2 is about.

ee2cf38bedde.say: Part two: what makes Kwen three point eight Flash Next different. It keeps the same loop from part one. It changes where the work and the memory go, so that a large model runs at a small model's cost. There are six changes.
ee2cf38bedde.heard: Part 2. What makes Quin 3.8 Flash Next different? It keeps the same loop from part 1. It changes where the work and the memory go, so that a large model runs at a small model's cost. There are six changes.

5a671d55459c.say: First, mixture of experts. Each layer has five hundred and twelve small feed-forward networks, and each token uses only ten of them, plus one shared expert.
5a671d55459c.heard: First, mixture of experts. Each layer has 512 small feed-forward networks, and each token uses only 10 of them, plus one shared expert.

be046099dff1.say: Second, hybrid layers. Thirty-six of the forty-eight layers use Gated Delta Net, a fixed-size memory. Only twelve keep a K V cache.
be046099dff1.heard: Second, hybrid layers. 36 of the 48 layers use gated Delta Net, a fixed-size memory. Only 12 keep a KV cache.

c299f2452a5e.say: Third, sparse attention. Those twelve layers read at most about two thousand past tokens, chosen by a cheap index.
c299f2452a5e.heard: Third, sparse attention. Those 12 layers read at most about 2,000 past tokens chosen by a cheap index.

bd8ef76f6c99.say: Fourth, hyper-connections: several residual streams instead of one, with learned mixing between them.
bd8ef76f6c99.heard: Fourth, hyperconnections. Several residual streams instead of one, with learned mixing between them.

5fa8c97034fd.say: Fifth, a phrase table: a thirty-five point eight gigabyte lookup table, keyed by a hash of the last few tokens, and added to one layer.
5fa8c97034fd.heard: Fifth, a phrase table, a 35.8GB lookup table keyed by a hash of the last few tokens and added to one layer.

c5b64d10b60e.say: And sixth, a vision encoder that turns images into tokens, and a draft head that guesses several tokens ahead. Let's take them one at a time.
c5b64d10b60e.heard: And sixth, a vision encoder that turns images into tokens, and a draft head that guesses several tokens ahead. Let's take them one at a time.

c2713d12d9ed.say: Change one: mixture of experts. In a plain model, every token goes through the same big feed-forward network. Here, that network is cut into five hundred and twelve small experts per layer.

751dd68ebbe3.say: A tiny router scores all five hundred and twelve for the current token, and runs only the top ten. One shared expert always runs as well. Think of a hospital with five hundred and twelve specialists, and a triage nurse: you see ten of them, plus a general practitioner who sees everyone.

39b6a5934da2.say: So the model stores a lot of knowledge, but uses about two percent of its experts per token. That's the label: one hundred and twenty-five B, A six B. One hundred and twenty-five billion weights in total, about six billion active per token.

5b360795bb44.say: Why do this? A bigger feed-forward network knows more, but every token pays for all of it. Running only the best-matching few gives the knowledge of one hundred and twenty-five billion weights, for the cost of about six billion. It works because the router is trained together with the experts: experts drift toward specialties, and the router learns which one is good at what.

d9e75209ef39.say: Full attention keeps a K V cache, one row per past token, and it grows forever. Delta Net keeps a fixed-size state instead. It's the same size at token ten, and at token two hundred thousand.
d9e75209ef39.heard: Full Attention keeps a KV cache, one row per past token, and it grows forever. DeltaNet keeps a fixed size state instead. It's the same size at token 10 and at token 200,000.

8e614f681319.say: Each new token does three things to that state. It fades old content a little. It corrects what's stored under its key. Then it reads with its query. The cost per token stays flat, no matter how long the text gets.
8e614f681319.heard: Each new token does three things to that state. It fades old content a little. It corrects what's stored under its key. Then it reads with its query. The cost per token stays flat, no matter how long the text gets.

6b41accd8d77.say: Think of a meeting. Full attention keeps the whole transcript. Delta Net keeps a whiteboard: it smudges old notes, and overwrites the entry for the current topic. Mixing both gives a cheap running summary, plus exact recall every fourth layer.
6b41accd8d77.heard: Think of a meeting. Full Attention keeps the whole transcript. DeltaNet keeps a whiteboard. It smudges old notes and overwrites the entry for the current topic. Mixing both gives a cheap running summary, plus exact recall every fourth layer.

439072f8ddb7.say: Why do we do this? Full attention compares each new token against every earlier one, so each token costs more as the text grows. Delta Net squeezes the past into a fixed-size matrix. It works because fading makes room for new content, and writing only the error means a fact stored twice isn't stored double.
